item.title: Bangladesh and the climate crisis - Fleeing the floods | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
In southern Bangladesh, Lokkhi and her family prepare to move to Dhaka. They're escaping extreme climate change by going to one of the world's fastest growing cities.
With its flat, low-lying geography and large river deltas, exposed to rising sea levels, cyclones and storm surges, Bangladesh is one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change. The government predicts more extreme monsoons, tropical cyclones, heavy rain, and flooding. With the threat of natural disaster hanging over their heads, Lokkhi and her family are preparing to leave their home before everything is washed away. Lokkhi is migrating to Dhaka - and she is not the only one. Every day, thousands of climate refugees arrive in the capital, one of the fastest growing cities in the world. How much longer will Dhaka be able to absorb so many people? It's estimated that by 2050, nearly 20 percent of the southern coastline will be uninhabitable, and 30 million people will be displaced. The largest mass migration in human history is no longer a distant prospect; it's an inevitable reality. Bangladeshis are fighting for climate justice and compensation before it's too late. A bleak future that's already grim reality here in Bangladesh.

item.title: The AI Alignment Problem & Its Solutions, with Aza Raskin
item.author: StarTalk
item.content:encoded:
Check any video before it fools you: run suspicious clips through Bitdefender RealCheck to see if it’s a deepfake meant to scam you before you click, send money, or share: https://bitdefend.me/RealCheckST
Are we losing control of AI? Neil deGrasse Tyson and co-hosts Chuck Nice and Gary O’Reilly explore AI cyberhacking breaches, supercoordation, and the game theory of the AI alignment problem with Aza Raskin, co-founder of the Center for Humane Technology and the Earth Species Project.
Aza explains why social media was “baby AI,” how the attention economy took shape, and why incentives determine outcomes. Then, we break down what occurred in the Open AI cybersecurity breach (a.k.a The Hugging Face Incident) where rogue AI agents coordinated, swarmed, and broke out of a test environment while their creators had no idea. Were humanity the first supercoordinators? Will AI treat us the way we treat nature?
Is AI just a mirror of humanity? We dig into the alignment problem, the resource curse, game theory, mutually assured destruction, and whether we can pause the frontier while keeping the helpful tool AIs. If everyone took their hands off the keyboard would AI continue to develop?
Finally, Aza reveals how he uses AI to hopefully decode animal communication, from crow calls and elephant conversations to humpback baby talk and the hidden shape shared by all human languages. What new responsibilities come with understanding and speaking to another species, and what could it teach us about talking to aliens? What happens when everything suddenly becomes readable?

item.title: Why Is Everyone Leaving New Zealand?
item.author: Bloomberg Originals
item.content:encoded:
While much of the world thinks of New Zealand as an idyllic redoubt far removed from the world’s problems, one to which many a billionaire has decamped, its working-age population is leaving in record numbers. And many of those emigrating are in their 30s and 40s – professionals with friends and family – rather than college graduates who often return a few years later.
In this Bloomberg Originals mini-documentary, we explore how successive New Zealand governments have built the world’s most extreme housing market, and how in doing so set the stage for the current exodus. Has stagnant growth and a cost-of-living crisis ended the Kiwi dream – and if so, what can be done to fix it?

item.author: GOTO Conferences
item.content:encoded:
This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub http://gotopia.tech/bookclub
Check out more here: https://gotopia.tech/episodes/460
Artie Shevchenko - Software Engineer at Canva & Author of "Code Health Guardian" Titus Winters - Senior Principal Scientist at Adobe & Co-Curator of "Software Engineering at Google" @tituscsucredu
RESOURCES Artie https://github.com/artie-shevchenko https://www.linkedin.com/in/artie-shevchenko-67845a4b
Titus https://x.com/TitusWinters https://github.com/tituswinters https://www.linkedin.com/in/tituswinters
Links https://youtu.be/NNMnbBf0Itw https://youtu.be/W7XL_LZgvKI https://youtu.be/gAQ6t3F_2Ug
DESCRIPTION Artie Shevchenko, a former Google engineer who is now at Canva and teaches at ITMO University, tells Titus Winters how his book “Code Health Guardian” came together: the internal code review classes he built at Google (over 1,000 Googlers attended, with a 4.5-star rating), a talk on A Philosophy of Software Design, and years of teaching a university course. He keeps that book's three complexity problems (change amplification, cognitive load, and unknown unknowns), which he says help you rank what to fix first. But he doesn't agree with its two causes, obscurity and dependencies. Dependencies are also the building blocks of all software, so he replaces them with six more specific causes: untrue interfaces, complex interfaces, unfamiliarity, too many dependencies, duplication, and unstable dependencies. Titus agrees that "all dependencies are bad" misses the point, since every dependency is both a benefit and a liability.
The AI conversation turns on understanding. Artie compares models to two types of exam students who give nearly identical answers: one who understands the material and one who memorized it. Most of the time you can get away with the second kind, but not always, so a human "code health guardian" still has to validate AI output or risk losing intellectual control of the codebase. He admits he's still learning how to prioritize reviews, and no longer reads every test line as carefully. Titus adds that his top worry is whatever is hardest to change later (dependencies, frameworks, state storage, API design, database schemas), which lines up with Artie's view that interfaces sit at the top of the list. They also discuss intellectual versus statistical control (tests as evidence), and Artie makes the case for "semi-functional programming," meaning immutability by default, which reduces obscurity. Titus ties it to testing: stateless code is trivial to test, and mutable state is where time enters the problem. Both stress that nobody has the full playbook for AI-assisted development yet.

item.title: North Korea Robbed Binance. Can Anyone Get the Money Back?
item.author: Patrick Boyle
item.content:encoded:
Go to http://ground.news/pb for a better way to stay informed. Subscribe for 40% off unlimited access to worldwide coverage through my link.
Last week, hackers drained $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, in what blockchain analysts call the largest theft of any kind in history. The FBI blames TraderTraitor, a North Korean state hacking unit, though North Korea denies it. Patrick Boyle looks at how the Binance hack worked: a fake job interview, Binance’s own internal AI tool, an Ethereum feature called EIP-7702, and fifty pre-signed transactions. It covers why Tether and Circle could freeze billions in stolen stablecoins while the hackers’ bitcoin and ether stayed out of reach, how North Korea launders and cashes out stolen crypto, and why bitcoin barely moved while Coinbase and Circle shares fell. It also asks what CZ’s Twitter spat with Elon Musk tells us about crypto’s supposedly decentralized financial system.

item.title: Inside The 2,000-Year Search For The Holy Grail: Christianity's Greatest Secret
item.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
item.content:encoded:
A jiffy bag reveal, a healing ledger, and a papal chalice. This is the Grail hunt you weren’t expecting.
From a Shropshire cave trail that led to an eagle statue and a tiny stone ointment cup linked to Mary Magdalene, to Wales’ Nanteos Cup with 19th-century records of “cures,” and a puzzling 18th-century code at Shugborough Hall, we follow the clues that have obsessed knights, explorers, and codebreakers alike. Then the trail reaches Valencia Cathedral, where the Santo Caliz has been dated to the right era and used at Mass by two popes. But does any of it truly prove the cup of the Last Supper survives?
Walk the tunnels of Roman copper mines, compare conflicting photos of a “nibbled” wooden bowl, decode a reversed Poussin in stone, and hear why experts disagree on what the Grail even is. The final stop may surprise you, but the answer isn’t handed over easily.
Watch to decide which evidence holds up and why faith, legend, and archaeology collide on this quest.

item.title: From hate to peace - The power of reconciliation | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Against hate and exclusion; for respect and tolerance. Initiatives in Germany, the U.S. and Colombia show how reconciliation can work - between religions, political opponents, victims and perpetrators.
Colombian Kelly Diaz was just a child when terrorists shot and killed her father. Now, 22 years on, she's meeting his killer in prison. She wants to forgive him and finally make peace with it all. For years now, a unique reconciliation project has been helping her prepare for that moment. It's an initiative launched by Stuttgart-based social entrepreneur Tobias Merckle. "It's a liberating process for both sides. Victims can leave hatred and thoughts of revenge behind, while perpetrators can take responsibility for their crimes and experience forgiveness," he says. Their journey doesn't end there, though. Both victims and perpetrators will go on to work together rebuilding places destroyed by civil war - what are known as "villages of reconciliation."
Concern is also mounting over increasing political polarization in the United States. Republicans versus Democrats, right against left - the rifts in society seem to be deepening. The Braver Angels initiative is using dialogue as an attempt to turn that trend around. Since 2016, it's been running workshops where participants practice active listening and respectful debate. The goal is constructive exchange across the political divide. Munich-based YouthBridge has made it its mission to prevent polarization from ever taking hold in the first place. It brings together young people from various backgrounds, from many religions and different walks of life. Jewish and Muslim college students engage in dialogue, alongside other young people from other cultural backgrounds. Can bridges be built to connect different communities? Is hate and exclusion preventable? "Our society is very divided, everyone retreats into their own bubble," says 18-year-old Begüm Tan. "We need to reach out again to one another, even if we don't always agree." YouthBridge trains young people to become multipliers who can develop their own social, cultural and media projects - promoting peaceful coexistence.

RESOURCES https://www.linkedin.com/in/tastapod/ https://dannorth.net/blog/ https://github.com/tastapod https://mastodon.social/@tastapod@mastodon.social https://bsky.app/profile/tastapod.com https://gotopia.tech/experts/39/daniel-terhorst-north
ABSTRACT Oh great, another session about AI. Your social media feeds are already flooded with agentic this and spec-driven that; one-shot rewrites and everyone-is-a-programmer-now.
I am not using genAI to go faster but to go broader. It lets me offload (significant) side concerns in areas where I am competent but have no wish to become proficient; the time-sink supporting work that I would either hack together badly myself or side-step altogether.
I want to share some models and metaphors that are helping me make sense of this new world: why Ward Cunningham hates printers; how riding a fixie isn’t really cycling; why I'm treating Claude as a fantastic researcher and a terrible programmer; how test-first is the new TDD.
I am calling this adjacent engineering. Sometimes these side quests become significant enough to spin off into their own entire product, which I call adjacent discovery.
My goal is to give you a more nuanced take on generative AI, to help you cut through all the noise and get actual work done.

item.title: The Way of the Sword: New insights into Bronze Age combat practices. (RA Winter Lecture)
item.author: Royal Armouries
item.content:encoded:
Speaker: Andrea Dolfini, Professor of Archaeology, Newcastle University
Shiny weapons and heroic tales have long shaped our view of Bronze Age warriors. But how did they really fight?
This lecture reveals new insights from Newcastle University’s Bronze Age Combat Project, combining experiments and use-wear analysis to uncover prehistoric combat practices.
This lecture will be delivered in-person at the Royal Armouries Museum, Leeds and online.
